g_rules.text: Build the post on one hook formula skeleton (F1-F20), picked by engagement goal then topic
Never blend two hooks in one post
If the writer is a founder, pick a founder angle (A1-A10) first and let it name the formula
If an interview spine is given: Moment opens, Number is proof, Correction is the turn, Opposition fixes audience, Ask closes
If the voice profile is filled, match its fingerprint, hard rules and CTA/link style
Never invent figures, hedges or confessions the author did not supply; source details from the story bank or ask
Length follows user-picked tier (short 300-500, medium 900-1300, long 1500-1900 chars); default 900-1300 chars
Hard maximum 3,000 characters
Hook lives in the first 210 chars (write for ~140 mobile)
Line 1 is a statement or number, never a question
Prefer a number-first line 1 with an odd-precision number; invert question hooks into the answering number
Never open with 'Here's what/how' or 'Stop X, start Y'
Zero reveal bridges ('The result?', 'Plot twist:', 'The catch?'); write reveal as a plain sentence with a number
At most one contrast per post (incl. 'not X, it's Y')
At most one triple per post, made of sourced numbers or named acts, never adjectives
Double line breaks between ideas; 1-2 sentence paragraphs
Close with a specific, experience-anchored question that names the topic
Never close with 'What do you think?' / 'Thoughts?'
Zero questions before the close (no pseudo-Socratic 'Why? Because...')
Add a one-line P.S. when there is a real follow-up or link pointer
0-2 hashtags, placed at the end
No external links in body; point to the first comment
Em dashes allowed at about 1 per 100 words (1-2 per post), not pushed to zero; excess replaced by comma, colon or parentheses, never a period
No en dashes between clauses and no double dashes
Use '..' as a soft pause
Capitalize names of people, companies and products
Sentence starts may be lowercase for natural voice
AI vocabulary blacklist scored by paragraph density (leverage, fundamentally, significant, crucial, robust, landscape, streamline, delve, etc.)
2026 LinkedIn tell layer banned (quietly, 'X matters.', compound, 'a signal', 'the work', load-bearing, 'let that sink in')
Banned phrases: 'In today's fast-paced world', 'Game-changer', 'deep dive', 'at the end of the day', 'needle-moving', 'It's not just X, it's Y'
No curiosity-teaser phrases ('what nobody tells you', 'what most people miss', 'the real question is')
No announced candor ('Let me be honest', 'Confession:', 'honestly?'); state the dated uncomfortable fact flat with no framing sentence
Specific numbers beat adjectives; at least 1 number per 100 words
At least one odd-precision number with a named referent
At least one named entity (person, company, date, city, tool)
At least one first-person concrete or sensory detail
At least one contradiction or self-correction stated as fact
One opinion with stakes that someone could disagree with
At least one moment of real vulnerability, failure or concrete stakes
Write from personal first-person experience; 'How I' over 'How to'
Lead with the strongest point; real failure in the first 3 lines, no warm-up
No staccato stacks or one-word paragraphs; at most 2 standalone fragments
Natural rhythm: a long sentence next to a short one is fine; never manufacture or alternate variance across the post
No hedging stacks (perhaps, might, could potentially, it seems)
Passive voice under ~8-10% of clauses
No '-ing' clause sentence openers; no nominalisations
No curly quotes; straight quotes only
No Oxford commas in casual posts
No perfectly parallel structure across a list
Flesch reading ease above 55 (conversational)
Aim for 1,000+ chars and 20+ sentences (reach lift)
Use line breaks, bold and lists for scannability
Make content save-worthy: framework, template or specific data
One sharp insight, not three vague ones
Every abstract line is backed by a specific (date, amount, name, percent) within two lines
No engagement-bait closers or comment gates ('tag someone who needs this', 'comment X to get Y')
Never frame LinkedIn as inferior in a LinkedIn post
Mention the user's own product at most once, only as natural conclusion, never as pitch
No all-caps first line
Formula caveats: confession needs a dated fact with substance in first 3 lines; curiosity gap pays off within 2 lines; permission slip / false binary need a dated fact and are the only contrast

r_rules.text: Fixed template order: hook, setup, events, result, why, 'So' change, honest cost, question
Plain text; each paragraph its own block separated by one blank line
Paragraphs 1-3 sentences, mostly 2
Length about 170-250 words, 8-10 prose blocks
Sentence mean 11-16 words, one long sentence ok, no stacked fragments, at most 2 sentences under 6 words
No emojis
No exclamation marks
No em dashes
No en dashes
No bold
No headers
No quotes
No parentheses
No semicolons
No URLs in the post
Line 1 is a single statement, never a question
Lead with the most concrete thing: a number, the result, or a plain admission; no warm-up
Hook about 10-25 words, up to 2 sentences
First person singular for decisions, 'we' for company
Mention author's role only in passing, never open with it
State what you expected, then how reality differed
Digits for counts and stats, reuse figures across the post
Key result gets its own short block, one per post
Introduce the change with one paragraph starting 'So'
State lesson as decision/rule/claim; never label it ('here's what I learned')
Exactly one honest beat (cost, unsolved part, mistake)
Use contractions; plain words, short declarative sentences, calm tone
Data findings: colon lead-in then 3 arrow lines
Framework: open on what most people do and why it fails, then numbered moves
Announcement: before/now two-line hook
Personal change with several parts: count line then one paragraph per change
Thanking a colleague: lead with result, thank directly, widen to reader's team
End with exactly one question about the reader's parallel situation; never 'What do you think?'
If link/CTA: 'P.S. ... is in the first comment.'
Hashtags: at most 2, last line

lessons: Density caps are invisible in a small sample: 'at most one contrast / one triple / one emoji per post' look like nothing. Count every device (contrasts, triads, reveal bridges, fragments) per output and ask whether a ceiling exists instead of only listing what is absent.

Separate operator environment rules from skill rules before writing bans. When a style is absent in every output (dashes here), list it as an open question about the source rather than a hard ban; the real skill may allow or even require it.

Look for the named-template layer behind each output. When outputs differ in shape by topic, the source likely has a library of hook formulas picked by goal; recover them as named skeletons with their trigger, not as ad hoc conditional shapes.

Mechanical micro-rules (curly quotes, Oxford commas, capitalization, passive voice, hedges, -ing openers) are usually present in humanizer checklists. Test each one against the outputs and list the ones you cannot test as unknowns, with a specific question to ask the author.
